council-hall.name: Hall of the Three Lanterns
council-hall.detail: An unclaimed stone meeting hall where three dragon clans pledged peace; the original letter and directions were written here.

copper-ridge.name: Coppercrest Ridge
copper-ridge.detail: Wind-cut copper rocks overlook the closed Sunspan crossing; a torn braid has been mistaken for a clan badge.

reed-channel.name: Reedmist Landing
reed-channel.detail: Marsh boats and ferry records show who could—and could not—have crossed the channel that morning.

highmist-watch.name: Highmist Weather Watch
highmist-watch.detail: A lofty bell platform reports sudden wind hazards, but its old clock is six minutes slow.

courier-roost.name: Wayfarer Courier Roost
courier-roost.detail: The neutral messenger guild stores emergency directions and a signed amendment to the peace letter’s route.

lantern-archive.name: Quiet Lantern Archive
lantern-archive.detail: Behind thick stone doors, a neutral keeper records sealed documents placed into storm-safe storage.

texts.1-2: The three dragon clans wrote a peace letter. Their leaders put three marks on it. The letter is for everyone.
texts.3-5: The original peace letter promises that Coppercrest, Reedmist, and Highmist will share safe passage through the valley. Each leader pressed a different mark into the wax. The treaty belongs to all three clans, not to any one leader.
texts.6-8: The signed peace letter pledges mutual access to valley crossings after years of distrust. Coppercrest adds a sun-stripe seal, Reedmist a reed-loop, and Highmist a cloud spiral; these marks appear together on the same document. Later rumors treat individual colors as evidence of ownership, yet the primary source establishes collective authorship. Its three seals were intended to symbolize equal standing, not competing claims.

1-2.q: How many clans agreed to the peace letter?
a: Three
Two
One
1-2.h: Count the marks on the letter.
1-2.why: Three leaders each added a mark to the same peace letter.

3-5.q: Why are three marks pressed into the letter?
a: They show all three clans agreed.
They show a secret fourth clan.
They mark three different letters.
3-5.h: Notice who put each mark on the document.
3-5.why: The three marks document agreement among all three leaders.

6-8.q: What is the best interpretation of the three seals as symbols?
a: Each seal grants exclusive control of the letter.
They represent shared responsibility for the agreement.
They warn of an approaching storm.
6-8.h: Read what the leaders promised, not the rumors about color.
6-8.why: The primary source joins the three seals on one shared pledge, symbolizing equality and cooperation.

texts.1-2: The letter was supposed to reach the Beacon of Accord at ten. A dragon would read it aloud there.
texts.3-5: An official delivery order says the sealed letter must be read publicly at the Beacon of Accord at 10:00 a.m. The planned path crosses Sunspan Bridge. The paper describes the first plan, not what the courier later did during the storm.
texts.6-8: The council’s morning order directs a neutral courier to deliver the sealed peace letter by 10:00 a.m. to the Beacon of Accord, following Sunspan Bridge. An attached note states that a separately issued emergency protocol governs unsafe crossings. As a primary source for the intended route, the order is valuable; as evidence of the route actually completed, it is incomplete. This distinction explains why witnesses expected the courier at the beacon.

1-2.q: Where did the letter need to go first?
a: To a bakery
To the river cave
To the Beacon of Accord
1-2.h: Find the place named in the instruction.
1-2.why: The council expected the letter to reach the Beacon of Accord.

3-5.q: What can the delivery order prove?
a: The courier definitely crossed the bridge
The route planned before the storm
A clan hid the letter
3-5.h: A plan can change when a route closes.
3-5.why: The document establishes the intended route, not the path the courier later took.

6-8.q: Which limitation of this source is most important?
a: It records intended instructions, not the later emergency deviation.
Its author is unknown, so it cannot be used.
It proves the archive illegally received the letter.
6-8.h: Compare an initial directive with a later route amendment.
6-8.why: A pre-storm primary directive cannot by itself establish what happened once conditions forced a change.

texts.1-2: A gold thread is caught on the bridge rail. The thread could be from many cloaks.
texts.3-5: A gold thread hangs from the Sunspan railing. Coppercrest cloaks often have gold trim, but festival messengers from all three clans wear the same color on their peace-day sashes. One thread cannot identify who used the bridge.
texts.6-8: A single golden braid thread snags on Sunspan’s rail. Coppercrest patrols use similar trim, leading some spectators to accuse that clan. However, the peace festival issued identical gold-edged sashes to guests from all three territories. Without a distinctive weave, a verified date, or an eyewitness placing someone at the rail, the fiber offers weak identification evidence. Its resemblance encourages confirmation bias among already suspicious observers.

1-2.q: Can one gold thread tell who walked here?
a: Yes, it names the person.
Yes, it says where the letter is.
No, many cloaks have gold thread.
1-2.h: Read whether the thread is special.
1-2.why: The clue is shared by many sashes, so it cannot identify one person.

3-5.q: Why should detectives avoid blaming Coppercrest based on this thread?
a: Gold is never worn by dragons.
Other clans also wore gold-trimmed sashes.
The rail was made of wood.
3-5.h: Look for another possible source of the same thread.
3-5.why: Because many festival participants wore gold, the thread alone cannot prove a particular culprit.

6-8.q: Which additional evidence would most strengthen an identification based on the thread?
a: A rumor that Coppercrest likes gold
A poem about golden sunlight
A dated image showing an identifiable wearer losing that exact braid
6-8.h: Look for an independent way to connect the object to a specific person and time.
6-8.why: An independently dated and distinctive match would address the uncertainty that makes the lone thread weak evidence.

texts.1-2: The ferry did not cross the river after nine. The wind was too strong. No secret boat carried the letter then.
texts.3-5: A ferryperson recorded the last morning crossing at 8:47. After 9:00, strong gusts stopped every boat until late morning. Reedmist scouts suspected an unseen ferry carried the peace letter, but the signed manifest lists no departures during that time.
texts.6-8: The Reedmist ferry manifest, signed by two boatkeepers, records a final crossing at 8:47 a.m. and suspends all departures from 9:00 until 11:30 because of hazardous wind. A guard’s rumor alleges that the courier escaped by boat after the bridge closed, but no corresponding trip appears in this contemporaneous transport log. The log makes the claimed ferry route unlikely; it does not, by itself, reveal the actual alternate route.

1-2.q: Did the ferry cross after nine?
a: Yes, many times
Only at noon
No, it stopped
1-2.why: The manifest says no ferry left after nine in the relevant period.

3-5.q: Which claim does the ferry record challenge?
a: That a bridge exists nearby
That a secret boat carried the letter after nine
That the river is used for travel
3-5.h: Check the times of the recorded crossings.
3-5.why: The signed manifest records no trip at the time of the alleged escape.

6-8.q: Which conclusion is warranted by the signed manifest?
a: It identifies who eventually stored the letter.
It undermines the proposed post-9:00 ferry route but leaves other routes possible.
It proves the boatkeepers intentionally lied.
6-8.h: Ask what this log can rule out and what it cannot establish.
6-8.why: A transport record can refute an alleged departure without establishing where the courier went instead.

texts.1-2: Three bells rang when wind hit the bridge. The bells meant Stop! They did not mean War!
texts.3-5: At 8:55 a.m., the Highmist watch struck three chimes, the agreed signal to close Sunspan Bridge during dangerous wind. Some dragons thought the chimes called guards to catch the courier. The written signal code explains they were a safety warning.
texts.6-8: The watch officer’s annotated weather log records dangerous crosswinds at 8:55 a.m., followed by the standardized three-chime closure alarm. A Coppercrest scout interpreted those bells as a summons to seize the letter, while a Reedmist witness called them a warning of attack. The official signal key defines three chimes as “Sunspan unsafe: do not cross.” The same sound acquired sharply different meanings because witnesses brought clan fears to their interpretations.

a: The bridge was unsafe
A party began
The letter was stolen
1-2.why: The signal warned everyone not to cross during the high wind.

3-5.q: Why did witnesses disagree about the three chimes?
a: The bell made no sound.
The log was written years later.
They assumed meanings instead of checking the signal code.
3-5.h: Compare their guesses to the official code.
3-5.why: The standardized code gives the chimes one safety meaning, although fearful listeners guessed otherwise.

6-8.q: What best illustrates differing points of view in the chime accounts?
a: Three chimes must have three separate official meanings.
The same objective signal is interpreted through each clan’s anxieties.
The weather report is fiction because listeners disagree.
6-8.h: Separate the event from its interpretation.
6-8.why: Although the bell pattern was fixed, listeners filtered it through their fears and loyalties.

texts.1-2: The watch clock was six minutes slow. When it said 8:49, the real time was 8:55.
texts.3-5: A clockmaker wrote, “Watch tower clock runs six minutes behind council time.” That is why one witness recorded 8:49 for the storm chimes while the council report recorded 8:55. The two reports describe the same event using different clocks.
texts.6-8: A signed calibration note, posted before Treaty Eve, states that the Highmist tower clock lagged six minutes behind the synchronized council clock. Thus Orin’s observation of the alarm at tower-time 8:49 corresponds precisely to the weather clerk’s official timestamp of 8:55. Without this correction, the testimonies appear inconsistent; with it, the sequence aligns. A discrepancy in recorded time is not necessarily evidence of dishonesty.

1-2.q: If the slow clock says 8:49, what is the real time?
1-2.h: Add six minutes to the slow clock.

3-5.q: What explains the different times for the same alarm?
a: The watch clock ran six minutes slow.
A courier changed the log.
The weather began on two mornings.
3-5.why: Adjusting the watch time by six minutes reconciles both accounts.

6-8.q: Which method best resolves the apparently conflicting timestamps?
a: Convert tower time using the documented six-minute offset.
Reject the older witness automatically.
Average both clocks to 8:52.
6-8.h: A time difference has been measured precisely.
6-8.why: Correcting the watch clock to council time aligns both records without inventing a second alarm.

texts.1-2: The messenger rule says: If the bridge is unsafe, take the sealed letter to Quiet Lantern Archive. Keep it safe.
texts.3-5: Before Treaty Eve, all three clan leaders agreed to an emergency instruction: when Sunspan Bridge closes, a courier must not risk the crossing. Instead, the courier takes the sealed letter to the neutral Quiet Lantern Archive, where a keeper locks it in Vault Two until the council can collect it.
texts.6-8: The courier guild’s contingency protocol carries three approval marks dated a week before the ceremony. Clause Four states: “If Sunspan is closed by the three-chime weather alarm, divert the sealed dispatch to Quiet Lantern Archive, Vault Two; obtain a keeper’s countersignature; send a notice to the council.” This prospective agreement distinguishes an authorized safety diversion from an unauthorized change of custody. It also shows that no individual clan could secretly invent the rule on Treaty Eve.

1-2.q: Where should a courier take the letter if the bridge is unsafe?
a: Into the river
Quiet Lantern Archive
Back to Coppercrest
1-2.h: Find the place in the messenger rule.
1-2.why: All three clans agreed that the neutral archive was the safe backup destination.

3-5.q: Why is the backup route important?
a: It shows any courier may keep the letter.
It proves a clan ordered a secret attack.
It authorizes safe storage when Sunspan closes.
3-5.h: Notice why all three clans approved the rule in advance.
3-5.why: The backup route was agreed before the storm and directed the courier to a neutral keeper.

6-8.q: Which fact most directly weakens an accusation that the diversion violated the peace agreement?
a: Coppercrest had shiny scales.
The courier carried a gold ribbon.
All three leaders preapproved the emergency route.
6-8.h: Check when and by whom the protocol was approved.
6-8.why: Prior authorization by all three parties makes a safety diversion legitimate under the stated conditions.

texts.1-2: A map shows Tavi turned away from the closed bridge. The new path goes past the courier roost toward the archive.
texts.3-5: Tavi’s field map shows the original road to the Beacon of Accord crossed Sunspan. A pencil arrow marked “bridge closed” leads instead through Willow Switch, past the courier roost, and toward the Quiet Lantern Archive. The map shows a possible route, but its unsigned arrow needs another record to confirm a completed transfer.
texts.6-8: The courier’s working map preserves the intended path to the Beacon of Accord while adding an arrow through Willow Switch, away from the sealed Sunspan crossing and toward the neutral archive. The alteration explains why separate scouts glimpsed the same messenger from different directions. Because the map is only an annotated working copy, it suggests movement but lacks the evidentiary strength of a timestamped route amendment and a countersigned arrival record.

1-2.q: What did Tavi do at the closed bridge?
a: Cross the broken bridge
Turn toward the safe archive path
Throw the letter away
1-2.h: Follow the pencil arrow on the map.
1-2.why: The arrow points to a safe route away from the bridge.

3-5.q: What is the main limit of Tavi’s marked map?
a: It has no places marked.
The map belongs to an enemy clan.
The unsigned arrow does not prove delivery was completed.
3-5.h: A route plan is not the same as a signed record of arrival.
3-5.why: The working map shows an intended detour, but delivery requires corroboration.

6-8.q: How should detectives best use the annotated map?
a: Use it to formulate a route hypothesis, then test it against signed records.
Treat it as conclusive proof of who received the letter.
Ignore it because a map can never be evidence.
6-8.h: A working map offers direction but needs independent confirmation.
6-8.why: The map is a useful secondary step in reconstructing movement, not standalone proof of custody.

texts.1-2: Tavi wrote: “9:08. Bridge shut. I will take the sealed peace letter to Quiet Lantern Archive.” Tavi signed the paper.
texts.3-5: At 9:08 a.m., neutral courier Tavi signed a route change: “Three-chime closure at Sunspan. Letter R-7 diverted under Clause Four to Quiet Lantern Archive, Vault Two. Original seals unbroken.” This document names the courier, the reason for the detour, and the new destination.
texts.6-8: The contemporaneous guild amendment reads, “9:08 council time: Sunspan impassable after safety signal; per three-clan Clause Four, I, Tavi of Wayfarer Roost, reroute Dispatch R-7 to Quiet Lantern Archive, Vault Two, seal intact.” Tavi signs, records the original dispatch code, and leaves an identifying impression of the neutral messenger guild. Unlike speculation about a colored cloak, this primary document establishes the identity of the decision-maker, the authorized reason, and the declared destination.

1-2.q: Who signed the new route note?
a: Daro
Tavi
Orin
1-2.why: Tavi signed the route amendment at 9:08.

3-5.q: Which three facts does the signed note establish together?
a: Which dragon ate breakfast and what color the bridge was
Who changed the route, why, and the new destination
Who invented the treaty and who broke it
3-5.h: Notice the signer, the closure reason, and the archive name.
3-5.why: Tavi’s signed note documents the authorized diversion and planned safe destination.

6-8.q: Why is this document stronger than a scout’s accusation?
a: It was posted on a higher wall.
It uses more exciting language.
It is a timestamped firsthand statement tied to an approved policy and dispatch number.
6-8.h: Consider authorship, proximity to the event, and documentary detail.
6-8.why: The signed contemporaneous amendment directly records the courier’s action and cites the governing protocol.

texts.1-2: The archive keeper Sera wrote: “9:17. I got the peace letter from Tavi. Its three seals are safe. I put it in Vault Two.”
texts.3-5: At 9:17 a.m., keeper Sera signed the Quiet Lantern Archive intake slip. It says Tavi delivered Dispatch R-7 with all three clan seals intact. Sera placed it in Vault Two and signed beside Tavi’s mark. This second record proves the letter actually reached the safe destination.
texts.6-8: The original 9:17 a.m. custody receipt records the transfer of peace letter R-7 from neutral courier Tavi to archive keeper Sera. Both countersign, document all three intact seals, and assign the packet to Vault Two under the emergency-preservation protocol. This independent acceptance record corroborates Tavi’s amendment: what was planned at 9:08 was completed nine minutes later. Because the sealed letter entered neutral custody with no sign of tampering, claims of theft or forged substitution lack supporting evidence.

1-2.q: Where did Sera put the letter?
a: The river
Vault Two
The beacon
1-2.h: Read the place named in Sera’s note.
1-2.why: The archive receipt names Vault Two as the storage location.

3-5.q: What does the intake slip establish beyond Tavi’s route plan?
a: That a secret ferry was used
That the letter arrived with its seals intact
That Coppercrest stole the letter
3-5.h: A receiving signature records an actual handoff.
3-5.why: Sera’s countersigned receipt confirms delivery and the letter’s condition.

6-8.q: Why are the route amendment and archive receipt especially persuasive together?
a: They document separate stages: authorized diversion and independently verified custody.
Both are anonymous rumors about the same event.
One copies a story from the other with no new information.
6-8.h: Compare a departure decision to a receiver’s acknowledgment.
6-8.why: The independent receipt corroborates the amendment and completes a traceable chain of custody.

texts.1-2: “I saw gold thread by the bridge,” says Daro. “I thought Reedmist took our letter. But I did not see anyone take it.”
texts.3-5: Daro, a Coppercrest scout, says he discovered gold thread on the rail and heard three bells. “I assumed Reedmist sent a boat around the bridge,” he admits. “But I never saw a boat or the peace letter itself.” His loyalty to Coppercrest shaped his suspicion.
texts.6-8: “I heard three Highmist chimes and found a piece of festival braid beside Sunspan,” says Coppercrest scout Daro Flintwing. He acknowledges inferring that Reedmist ferried the peace letter away because his clan had argued with marsh leaders the previous season. Under questioning, he concedes he saw neither a courier leaving by boat nor the letter changing hands. His testimony is evidence that he encountered the thread and bells, not firsthand evidence of Reedmist wrongdoing.

1-2.q: Did Daro see someone steal the letter?
a: Yes, he saw it clearly.
Yes, Sera showed him.
No, he only guessed.
1-2.h: Daro says he did not see anyone take it.
1-2.why: Daro’s belief is a guess, not an observed theft.

3-5.q: Why may Daro’s accusation be unreliable?
a: He assumed guilt based on an old rivalry without seeing a theft.
He dislikes the sound of bells.
His boots were muddy.
3-5.h: Notice the difference between what he saw and what he believed.
3-5.why: His clan loyalty and past dispute may bias his interpretation of ordinary clues.

6-8.q: What is the most defensible use of Daro’s account?
a: It establishes Reedmist guilt beyond doubt.
It verifies a thread and alarm, while his theory of theft needs independent proof.
It invalidates the weather log.
6-8.h: Identify the portions based on direct observation.
6-8.why: Only Daro’s observed thread and bells are firsthand evidence; his accusation is an inference colored by conflict.

texts.1-2: “I saw a gold flash on the path,” says Valeena. “I thought it was Coppercrest. I did not see the letter.”
texts.3-5: Valeena says a gold-trimmed figure moved past Willow Switch after the bridge closed. She thought it must be a Coppercrest dragon because of the color. “I could not see the face, and our festival sashes were gold too,” she admits. No Reedmist ferry left at that hour.
texts.6-8: Reedmist boatkeeper Valeena Reedwhisper describes a brief gold flash on the Willow Switch path after the storm bells. She inferred the traveler was Coppercrest and therefore suspected that clan of diverting the letter. Yet fog obscured the face, festival sashes from every clan bore gold trim, and her signed ferry record shows no boat departed after 9:00. Her observations may help place an unidentified traveler near the alternate path, but they cannot establish clan identity or motive.

1-2.q: Could Valeena see the traveler’s face?
a: No
Yes
Only in a drawing
1-2.h: She saw only a flash of gold.
1-2.why: Valeena did not see the face, so she could not identify the traveler.

3-5.q: What is the strongest conclusion from Valeena’s statement?
a: Someone wearing gold passed Willow Switch, but their clan is unknown.
Coppercrest definitely stole the letter.
A ferry carried the letter away.
3-5.h: Look for the part she actually saw.
3-5.why: The visible flash suggests movement on the path, but gold trim was not unique to Coppercrest.

6-8.q: How does Valeena’s perspective affect her interpretation?
a: She has signed the archive receipt herself.
She turns an ambiguous color cue into an accusation against a rival clan.
She demonstrates the ferry was active during the storm.
6-8.h: Compare observation, assumption, and existing rivalry.
6-8.why: Her prior expectations shape the culprit she imagines, even though the evidence is not identifying.

texts.1-2: “I rang three bells when the wind grew strong,” says Orin. “My clock was slow. The bells meant stay safe.”
texts.3-5: Orin says the wind alarm sounded at 8:49 on his tower clock. Another report lists 8:55. “Our tower clock loses six minutes,” he explains. “Three chimes always mean the bridge is closed for safety. They are not a battle call.”
texts.6-8: Highmist watch officer Orin Cloudbell reports ringing three warning chimes at tower-time 8:49, exactly when the weather log lists the bridge closure as 8:55 council time. He points to a clockmaker’s written six-minute calibration offset and demonstrates the standard storm signal. Coppercrest and Reedmist observers heard the same bells but attributed them to hostile orders. Orin’s first-person account is corroborated by the calibration note and signal code, making his timing and stated action more credible than the rival interpretations.

1-2.q: Why did Orin ring the bells?
a: To warn of strong wind
To start a race
To hide the letter
1-2.h: He says the bridge was unsafe.
1-2.why: The bells warned travelers not to cross the bridge during the storm.

3-5.q: Why do Orin’s time and the council time differ?
a: He was describing a different day.
The letter changed the weather.
His tower clock was six minutes slow.
3-5.why: 8:49 on the tower corresponds to 8:55 council time.

6-8.q: Which evidence most effectively supports Orin’s reliability?
a: His clan’s reputation for having clear scales
The scout’s opinion that three bells meant war
The independently recorded clock offset and standardized weather-chime code
6-8.h: Look for records that can corroborate timing and meaning.
6-8.why: The offset and code verify both when the bells rang and what they officially signaled.

texts.1-2: “I carried the peace letter,” says Tavi. “The bridge closed, so I took it to the archive. I signed a route note.”
texts.3-5: Tavi, a neutral courier, says the Sunspan crossing closed just before she reached it. “All three leaders approved a safer path,” she explains. “I wrote a route amendment at 9:08 and carried the still-sealed letter to Quiet Lantern Archive. Ask the keeper for the arrival receipt.”
texts.6-8: Neutral courier Tavi Wayfarer reports approaching Sunspan after the three-chime closure, following the guild’s preapproved Clause Four rather than risking an unsafe crossing. She signed route amendment R-7 at 9:08 and says she handed the original sealed peace letter to archive keeper Sera nine minutes later. Her account has a clear incentive—defending her professional judgment—but is independently testable against the protocol, dated amendment, and archive custody record. Her testimony should therefore be corroborated rather than accepted on reputation alone.

1-2.q: What did Tavi do when the bridge closed?
a: She dropped the letter.
She sold the letter.
She took the letter to the archive.
1-2.why: Tavi followed the safe route approved by all three clans.

3-5.q: Which document could best verify Tavi’s claim that she delivered the letter?
a: The keeper’s signed intake receipt
Daro’s thread guess
A festival song about peace
3-5.h: Find a record made by the person receiving the letter.
3-5.why: The archive intake receipt independently documents the arrival Tavi describes.

6-8.q: Why should investigators check the intake receipt even though Tavi has a signed route amendment?
a: All messengers are untrustworthy.
The route amendment uses a cipher nobody can read.
A decision to reroute does not by itself prove the letter arrived.
6-8.why: Independent receiving documentation verifies custody after the rerouting decision.

texts.1-2: “Tavi brought me the peace letter,” says Sera. “I checked three seals and put it safely in Vault Two.”
texts.3-5: Keeper Sera remembers Tavi arriving at 9:17 with the sealed letter. “I checked every clan mark before we both signed the receipt,” she says. “The storm blocked our notice messenger for a while, so the council did not hear from us immediately.”
texts.6-8: Sera Lanternkeeper, the archive’s neutral custodian, describes receiving sealed Dispatch R-7 at 9:17. She and Tavi countersigned a record of the intact three-clan wax seals and its placement in Vault Two. Sera explains that a squall delayed the notice sent to the council, creating an information gap in which rumors spread. The delay is a failure of communication, not evidence of concealment; the dated, jointly signed intake document predates the council’s later accusation.

1-2.q: How many clan seals did Sera check?
a: Three
One
Two
1-2.h: All three leaders signed the letter.

3-5.q: Why did the council mistakenly think the letter was still missing?
a: Sera destroyed the letter.
Tavi never arrived.
The archive’s notice was delayed by the storm.
3-5.h: Read what happened to the message sent back.
3-5.why: A storm delayed the update even though the letter had already reached safe storage.

6-8.q: Which inference best reconciles the archive record with the council’s fears?
a: An interrupted communication channel allowed misinformation despite documented custody.
The letter must have been forged, since there was a delay.
Sera intentionally concealed the letter to claim ownership.
6-8.h: Separate the physical location of the letter from news of its arrival.
6-8.why: The contemporaneous receipt proves safe custody; the delayed message explains why other people remained uninformed.

case.title: The Dragon Council
case.subtitle: CASE FILE 011 • THREE CLANS, ONE LETTER
case.goal: Discover who authorized and carried out the emergency change in the peace letter’s route, where the letter was safely stored, and why it missed the public reading. Compare the perspectives of three clans and build a conclusion from firsthand records rather than rival accusations.

brief.1-2: Three dragon clans made a peace letter. The letter did not reach the big hill where everyone would hear it. Each clan thinks something different happened. Visit the bridge, river, watch tower, courier roost, and archive. Read the clues to find where the letter went.
brief.3-5: In the valley of Lumenreach, the Coppercrest, Reedmist, and Highmist dragon clans finally agree to peace. Their letter is meant to be read at the Beacon of Accord, but it never arrives on time. A storm closes the bridge, gold thread appears on the rail, and each clan suspects another. Investigate the official route, conflicting witness accounts, and emergency records to learn who changed the letter’s path, where it ended up, and why.
brief.6-8: In the wholly imagined valley of Lumenreach, three dragon clans—Coppercrest of the sunlit ridges, Reedmist of the wet lowlands, and Highmist of the cloud terraces—sign a historic shared-passage accord. Yet their sealed peace letter fails to appear at its scheduled public reading. Coppercrest blames a rival ferry, Reedmist suspects a gold-trimmed ridge messenger, and Highmist insists its warning chimes were misunderstood. The accusations reflect generations of mistrust, but a slower tower clock, a preapproved emergency route, and a traceable chain of custody suggest an entirely different explanation. Reconstruct the journey and decide which accounts reflect observations and which reflect fear.

theoryLabels.who: Who made and documented the emergency reroute of the peace letter?
theoryLabels.where: Where was Dispatch R-7 actually secured after the bridge closure?
theoryLabels.why: Why did the letter miss the public reading at the Beacon of Accord?

where.label: Beacon of Accord — public reading platform
Reedmist ferry hold — across the channel

why.label: A rival clan secretly stole the letter to stop peace.
A storm closed the crossing, activating the clans’ agreed safety diversion.
The courier sold the letter to a private collector.
The three chimes ordered guards to attack the messenger.
The archive keeper hid the letter to replace its seals.

feedback.who: Consider who physically controlled the sealed dispatch and signed the 9:08 change of route. Daro and Valeena report suspicions, Orin sounded the warning, and Sera received the packet. The SIGNED ROUTE AMENDMENT names the person who made the diversion.
feedback.where: The original delivery ORDER named the beacon, but it only states an intention. Look for the KEEPER’S RECEIPT at the neutral archive: it confirms exactly which vault accepted R-7 and whether its three seals were intact.
feedback.why: Separate clan rivalry from the condition that triggered Clause Four. Compare the THREE-CHIME STORM LOG with the previously signed NEUTRAL ROUTE RULE. Which documented hazard made the ordinary route unsafe?
feedback.proofs: Select BOTH Tavi’s Signed Route Amendment (the contemporaneous authorized reroute) AND the Countersigned Vault-Two Receipt (independent proof of completed custody). Other clues explain the confusion but cannot together establish both route and arrival.

resolution.summary: The peace letter was never stolen. Neutral courier Tavi Wayfarer followed the three-clan storm protocol and safely deposited the sealed dispatch in Quiet Lantern Archive’s Vault Two at 9:17 a.m.
resolution.outcome: The first peace ceremony nearly broke down because the three clans interpreted the same incomplete clues through old distrust. Coppercrest scout Daro mistook a shared festival braid for a rival badge and assumed Reedmist had used a secret ferry, even though the signed ferry manifest lists no departure. Reedmist boatkeeper Valeena saw a gold flash by Willow Switch and blamed Coppercrest without identifying the traveler. Highmist officer Orin sounded three chimes as a storm warning, not a call for war. His watch clock lagged six minutes, so accounts that first seemed contradictory describe one alarm at 8:55 council time. All three leaders had approved Clause Four, requiring a sealed dispatch to be diverted to a neutral archive whenever Sunspan was closed. Tavi recorded that decision in a signed route amendment at 9:08; keeper Sera independently acknowledged receipt of intact Dispatch R-7 at 9:17 and placed it in Vault Two. A weather-delayed message prevented the council from learning the news in time for the beacon reading. When the letter was finally displayed with its three seals intact, the leaders agreed to share verified records before making future accusations. The case demonstrates that differing perspectives can explain conflict, but trustworthy documents and fair inference can resolve it.

timeline.event: The three leaders approve the neutral courier guild’s Clause Four: unsafe Sunspan crossings require protected custody at Quiet Lantern Archive, Vault Two.
Coppercrest, Reedmist, and Highmist sign one peace letter R-7 in the Hall of the Three Lanterns.
Neutral courier Tavi receives the sealed document for a 10:00 public reading at the Beacon of Accord via Sunspan.
The final Reedmist ferry crosses; all later departures are canceled because of increasing wind.
Dangerous wind closes Sunspan Bridge. Orin sounds the official three-chime alarm; his six-minute-slow tower clock reads 8:49.
Tavi reaches the closed crossing, observes the warning, and turns toward Willow Switch rather than risking the bridge.
Tavi signs the dispatch R-7 route amendment, invoking the preapproved Clause Four diversion to Quiet Lantern Archive.
Archive keeper Sera and Tavi countersign the receipt confirming the intact letter is secured in Vault Two.
Daro and Valeena separately report a gold thread and a distant gold flash, then assume rival clans are involved.
The beacon reading cannot proceed; the archive notice is still delayed by storm conditions and rumors spread at the council.
The archive’s delayed message reaches the council, confirming neutral custody and the unbroken seals.
Representatives from all three clans verify the signed records and agree to announce the accord after the crossing reopens.
